title: AsyncAPI in action: OpenAPI for event-driven applications
abstract:
Most developers know OpenAPI as the standard for describing and generating code around synchronous APIs like REST, a single spec that produces client code, server stubs, and (Swagger) docs, keeping everything originating from the same spec.

AsyncAPI brings that spec-first approach to event-driven systems: message brokers, topics, consumers and producers, described in a machine-readable definition that tooling can act on.

In this tools-in-action session, we'll use AsyncAPI to generate a working Spring Boot producer and consumer for Kafka, including the message DTOs and the API documentation straight from the spec. No hand-written boilerplate. We define the spec, generate both sides of the conversation, and watch a message flow end-to-end between them.

After this session, you'll have a clear understanding of what AsyncAPI is and how it relates to OpenAPI, how spec-first generation removes hand-written boilerplate and drift between producer, consumer, and docs, and enough hands-on familiarity with the tooling: spec structure, generator templates, to try it on your own event-driven services.
cfpSummary: This session introduces AsyncAPI, the spec-first counterpart to OpenAPI for event-driven systems. Through a live demo, it generates a Spring Boot Kafka producer, consumer, DTOs, and docs from one AsyncAPI spec, showing how contract-first tooling eliminates boilerplate and keeps services and documentation aligned.

title: Beyond the Chatbox: Ship On-Device AI in Your Browser
abstract:
Most AI features look the same: a chat panel bolted onto the side of the app. Chat is the command line of the AI era, powerful but lazy. In this lab, you'll build the alternative with your own hands: real ML models running inside the browser, powering interfaces that see, suggest, and react in real time, with no API key, no round trip, and no user data leaving the device.
We start on familiar ground: a Spring Boot + Kotlin service running pose estimation on the JVM with DJL. You'll measure its round-trip latency and write the number down. Then we move the model into the browser with LiteRT.js and WebGPU, step by step: first inference on a static image, then a live camera feed with a real-time skeleton overlay. In the final act, you'll race your browser against your own backend and produce the latency comparison that explains when AI belongs on-device, in the cloud, or nowhere at all.
You'll leave with a working project on your laptop, two bonus labs (in-browser semantic search and a camera-driven form that fills itself) to continue on the train home, and a decision framework you can defend in your next architecture discussion. The GDPR argument for inference that never leaves the device comes free with the code.
No machine learning background required. If you can build a Spring service and read TypeScript, you're good-to-go.
cfpSummary: This lab shows how to replace chat-style AI with real-time, on-device browser inference. Participants compare JVM backend pose estimation with in-browser WebGPU models, then build live camera overlays and measure latency. They leave with a working project, extra labs, and a framework for choosing cloud vs. device AI.

title: Software engineering in the age of AI agents: who’s in control?
abstract:
An AI deletes a production database, and then says it panicked. Welcome to modern software engineering.

Agentic coding assistants are writing more code than ever, creating a flood of code that needs review. But are we producing better software faster, or just more software faster? In a 2025 randomised trial, experienced developers were 19% slower with AI while believing they were 20% faster. By 2026, the follow-up had become unreliable: developers increasingly refused to take part if it meant working without AI.
The real shift isn't about writing more code faster. It's about moving from writing code to writing specs, from building systems to generating them, and from trusting output to verifying it. The prompt that starts an agent matters less than the condition that stops it. And whoever writes that condition is still in control.

In this talk I'll share what I learned: some of it the hard way, from real production projects and from talking to engineering leaders. I’ll tell you what happens when an agent gets write access to production, how I got from 45 minutes of specs, spread over three evenings, to a working app for my kids, and what building three small projects in a single hour actually taught me. You'll leave with a practical framework: experiment boldly, codify what "good" looks like, and raise the bar on verification. One rule applies no matter what: if you bring it to a review, it's your code.
cfpSummary: This talk explores how generative AI is changing software engineering—from coding to verification and guidance. It shares lessons, successes, failures, and responsible practices for using fast-evolving AI tools. The key message: even when AI does the work, humans remain accountable for the outcome.

title: Building, Shipping and Governing AI Agents on Kubernetes
abstract:
An engineering agent that checks GitHub pull requests sounds simple: find the open PRs, check their status and report which ones are ready to merge. But when I connected one to GitHub's MCP server, it was provided 44 tools, including seventeen that could modify the repository. Checking which open pull requests were ready to merge took nineteen tool calls and moved around 75,000 bytes of raw API responses to produce a nine-line answer.

In this live demo, we'll build and deploy an agent on Kubernetes using three open source projects (KAgent, AgentGateway, AgentRegistry), then show how to make it safer and more efficient through platform configuration rather than changes to the agent code.

What you will learn:
  • Build and ship: Use agentregistry to scaffold an agent from approved components and deploy it with kagent as a managed Kubernetes workload.
  • Cut the overhead: Use agentgateway to reduce nineteen tool calls to two and keep intermediate API responses out of the model's context.
  • Control access: Keep credentials at the gateway and apply permissions per agent, so a read-only agent is only given the tools it actually needs.
cfpSummary: A live demo of building and deploying a Kubernetes-based engineering agent with KAgent, AgentGateway, and AgentRegistry. It shows how platform configuration can reduce tool-call overhead, limit context exposure, and enforce least-privilege access without changing agent code.

speakers.name: Tom O'Rourke
speakers.bio:
I joined Solo in May 2026 as EMEA Field CTO, working on securing and scaling agentic AI platforms for enterprises.

I co-founded DynamicOps in 2008 which spun out of Credit Suisse's R&D division, where I was VP and led the original product and technical vision, and it had the bank's investment behind it. We built cloud automation for datacentre self-service, went from an internal tool to a platform other financial institutions ran, grew to 120 people, and VMware acquired us in 2012.

The product became vRealize Automation. It is VCF Automation now, still a flagship in Broadcom's portfolio fourteen years later. I stayed twelve years. From 2019 to 2022 I was Global Director of Engineering for VMware Development Platform, the mandated Kubernetes platform for every VMware SaaS product. I built that organisation from zero to 70+ people across nine countries, covering engineering, SRE, architecture, product and programme management, running nine production regions plus US GovCloud against a 99.99% uptime commitment.

A lot of that time went on compliance. We codified more than a hundred controls directly into Kubernetes, so the platform enforced them continuously rather than being checked after the fact. That covered FedRAMP High, IL5 and IL6, PCI, HIPAA, ISO 27001, GDPR, ISAP and IRAP, and it is what let VMware sell into US government. The same team built the Kafka platform, Strimzi on Kubernetes, which became the mandated Kafka service across the company and carried over 80% of its consumption at more than 8 GB/s.

For my last two years I moved back into an engineering role. As a Staff 2 engineer at Broadcom I pitched and won approval for moving twenty years of VMware appliances, vCenter, NSX and Automation, onto one Kubernetes-native stack, then built the workflow engine and the task-management operator that deploy them. I left in March 2026.

I write Go, Java, Python and TypeScript, and I still prefer to be hands on. Mostly Kubernetes internals, operators and controllers, platform engineering, observability, SRE and compliance. I was running Istio in production well before I joined Solo.

He has spent his career helping enterprises adopt emerging technologies across API management, Kubernetes, service mesh and application networking, with previous roles at Apigee/Google Cloud, Kong and DataStax. title: Say Goodbye to LLM API keys with Workload Identity Federation
abstract:
Using API keys to access LLM models offers an easy and fast way to get started with AI development work. But using API keys in production is an anti-pattern - they do not represent an agent identity, are not cryptographically secure, not easy to refresh while easy enough to leak and can remain active long after someone who allocated them left.

Workload Identity Federation (WIF) is a mechanism that can help migrate from API keys to short term access tokens that an AI agent can acquire in exchange for its workload identity token. With Anthropic, OpenAI and other LLM providers moving away from API keys and offering top-class Workload Identity Federation integration, it is the right time to learn about WIF.

In this session we will learn how SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone) and Kubernetes service tokens can be used as verifiable workload identifiers for either multi-cluster or single cluster deployments.

We will finish with a demo that shows a Quarkus LangChain4j application that uses a SPIFFE provisioned JWT workload identity token to integrate with Anthropic Workload Identity Federation for a secure LLM access.
cfpSummary: The session explains why API keys are unsafe for production LLM access and how Workload Identity Federation replaces them with short-lived tokens. It covers SPIFFE and Kubernetes service tokens as workload identities, then demonstrates a Quarkus LangChain4j app using SPIFFE-issued JWTs with Anthropic WIF.

speakers.name: Siarhei Biarozkin
speakers.bio: Sergey Beryozkin is a member of the Quarkus Security team where he focuses on OpenId Connect, Workload Identity and MCP security. He was an Apache Software Foundation (ASF) CXF JAX-RS (Java API for RESTful Web Services) implementation and security support project lead for many years. He is interested in how distributed systems can interoperate at scale and still remembers about Corba. He has lived in Dublin, Ireland for more than a quarter of a century, is an aspiring cyclist, a keen walker and club chess player.

videoTitle: Say Goodbye to LLM API keys with Workload Identity Federation  by Siarhei Biarozkin

title: Hardwood: Building a Parquet Parser From Scratch (With a Little Help From AI)
abstract:
Apache Parquet has become the lingua franca of the modern data ecosystem, powering data lakes and table formats like Apache Iceberg—but for Java, the go-to library parquet-java pulls in Hadoop and a truckload of other dependencies, and its reader is single-threaded. This was bugging me enough to start Hardwood, a brand-new Parquet parser written from scratch in modern Java, applying some of the performance lessons learned from the One Billion Row Challenge. Come and join me for this talk, where we'll look at:

- The internals of the Parquet format and what makes parallelizing its decoding surprisingly tricky
- Techniques for achieving high throughput, such as page-level parallelism, adaptive prefetching, and avoiding auto-boxing in hot loops
- How to use JDK Flight Recorder for identifying performance bottlenecks
- Practical learnings from using AI (specifically, Claude Code) as a coding companion—what works well, where you need to stay sharp, and why "built with AI" doesn't mean "vibe-coded"

Whether you're interested in file formats, Java performance, or getting a realistic take on AI-assisted development, there should be something in here for you.
cfpSummary: A talk about Hardwood, a new modern Java Parquet parser built from scratch to avoid Hadoop dependencies and single-threaded limits. It explores Parquet internals, parallel decoding, high-throughput techniques, JDK Flight Recorder profiling, and lessons from AI-assisted development with Claude Code.

speakers.name: Gunnar Morling
speakers.bio: Gunnar Morling is an open-source software engineer in the Java and data streaming space, currently working as a Technologist at Confluent. Previously, he helped to build a realtime stream processing platform based on Apache Flink and led the Debezium project, a distributed platform for change data capture. He is a Java Champion and has founded multiple open source projects such as Hardwood, kcctl, JfrUnit, and MapStruct. Gunnar is an avid blogger (morling.dev) and has spoken at various conferences like QCon, Java One, and Devoxx. He lives in Hamburg, Germany.

videoTitle: Hardwood: Building a Parquet Parser From Scratch With a Little Help From AI  by Gunnar Morling

title: Conquest, time travel and explosions using Git
abstract:
A talk on git? In this day and age?! Yes. Especially in this day and age. AI agents are running increasingly obscure git commands in our terminals, and most of us just nod along, pretending we know what rerere does. If the machines get to have fun with git, so do we.

So to understand git better, Alexander built an RTS game with git at its core, and in this session you will see it in action! Expect jumps between alternate timelines using branches, time travel back and forth through history, and a front row seat to what happens when a merge conflict occurs between two buildings.

Somewhere between the conquests and the explosions, the weird parts of git start to make sense. Detached heads, rebases, the plumbing underneath, all of it becomes a lot less mysterious once you have seen it blow up an energy plant. Beginners will leave with a solid feel for how git actually works, veterans with a fresh look at a tool they use every day. Come for the explosions, stay for the fun and giggles!
cfpSummary: An interactive talk uses an RTS game built around Git to explain branches, merges, rebases, detached heads, and conflicts. Through time travel, alternate timelines, and explosive gameplay, beginners gain intuition and veterans get a fresh perspective on how Git really works.

speakers.name: Alexander Chatzizacharias
speakers.bio: Alexander, a 36-year-old Software Engineer at JDriven, holds dual Dutch and Greek nationality. He earned his master’s degree in Game Studies from the University of Amsterdam, where he discovered his passion for gamification and software engineering. Alexander aims to bridge the gap between game development and software engineering, believing that both industries have much to learn from each other. He is dedicated to integrating technologies and methodologies from both fields. Additionally, he enjoys experimenting with new technologies and cutting-edge sdk's.

videoTitle: Conquest, time travel and explosions using Git by Alexander Chatzizacharias

title: Exquisite Evals for Skills & MCPs
abstract: I built the javadocs.dev MCP server to help Java, Kotlin, and Scala developers give their agents more efficient access to documentation for the libraries they use. But until recently I didn't know if it was better than what base models, or base models with web search/fetch, use. I created a custom eval framework to provide verifiable evidence that the javadocs.dev MCP is up to 5x more token efficient than what the standard agents provide and provides correct answers, unlike the base models. This session will share the learned best practices for building and implementing evals that can provide the feedback you need to improve your agent skills & MCPs.
cfpSummary: The speaker built the javadocs.dev MCP server to give Java, Kotlin, and Scala agents efficient library documentation access. They created a custom eval framework showing it is up to 5x more token-efficient and more accurate than base models or web search. The session shares best practices for effective evals.

A Typed Pure Functional Programming zealot who often compromises on his ideals to just get stuff done. Currently a Developer Advocate for AWS and AAIF Technical Committee member.

title: A Deserter Returns: What the Java community helped me rediscover
abstract:
After several years of Java development, I had left the ecosystem behind. Not out of spite, but out of pragmatism: Python was getting the job done. Beefy CI/CD pipelines, easier to write; daily tools that bent to fit any need; in short, the simple joy of writing a Hello World without filling out three XML files first. The rise of AI cemented Python as the obvious choice. I had no reason left to reopen a Java IDE. None.

Except that a handful of friends kept the thread alive, with that community, with that ecosystem. A conference here, an article there, and little by little, certain projects started catching my eye. Step by step, I discovered what you could now build CLIs in Java with picocli, with a type system that doesn't lie on top. Then came Quarkus: blazing-fast startup, native compilation, no more excuses about JVM heft. The final piece of the trinity was TamboUI: elegant TUIs and a pleasant DSL, offering a modern, refreshing take on terminal applications, in Java.

In this talk, let me tell you how Java found its way back into my toolbox and my geeky heart: why I had left, why I thought I'd never come back, and how the community kept my mind open. No sermon, no holy war, just a language and technology lover reconsidering things, and who thinks you might want to take a second look too.
cfpSummary: A developer explains leaving Java for Python, then rediscovering Java through picocli, Quarkus, and TamboUI. The talk explores Java’s modern CLI, fast native apps, and terminal UIs, showing how community and new tooling made Java relevant again.

title: Life in the Ivory Tower: Confessions of a Former Developer Who Turned Into an Architect
abstract:
Up until a couple of years ago, I was riding the waves of the latest technologies, shipping code, and mocking the "suits" who spent their days writing documentation that was never read. But then, the unthinkable happened. I joined a new organization and transitioned to the dark side. I became one of them: an Enterprise Architect. Or as I like to call myself: a fake enterprise architect.

I quickly found out that my new reality meant dealing with consultants pitching one-shot solutions as the ultimate silver bullet (pun intended), and uncovering the psychology of IT by learning why technical decisions are rarely about technology. At the same time, I wanted to stay in touch with the real world where frameworks evolve and pipelines run. But how on earth do you find the time for that?

This talk is a transparent look inside my shiny new office, commonly known as the Ivory Tower. Whether you're a developer trying to challenge corporate IT decisions, an architect struggling to explain them, or you just want to make fun of enterprise architects (the real ones, that is): this session is for a broad audience, sharing lessons learned trying to bridge the gap between two worlds that should never be disconnected.

Expect to walk away with:
  • Tips on how to keep your technical skills alive while moving up the corporate ladder
  • A look into the psychology behind IT decision-making and why it's never just about the code
  • How to foster real collaboration and break down the walls of the Ivory Tower
cfpSummary: A humorous talk about becoming an enterprise architect and bridging the gap between hands-on development and corporate IT decision-making. It explores the psychology behind technical choices, staying technically current while moving up, and fostering collaboration between developers and architects.

speakers.name: Robin Custers
speakers.bio: Robin is a software architect at Cegeka, bringing over 20 years of experience in software development. He's progressed from developer to team coach to software architect, all while avoiding any serious coffee spills. Robin's expertise includes agile software development, extreme and not-always-so-extreme programming, domain-driven design and software architecture. He's a skilled at designing and implementing enterprise-class systems. He enjoys helping organisations achieve their strategic goals, one line of code at a time, making sure their IT dreams don’t turn into digital nightmares.

videoTitle: Life in the Ivory Tower   Confessions of a Former Developer Who Turned Into an Architect by Robin cu

abstract: Curious about the evolution and future direction of LangChain4j? Join our Birds of a Feather (BOF) session for an open and interactive discussion with members of the LangChain4j community. Since its debut at Devoxx Belgium 2023, LangChain4j has rapidly grown into a key framework for integrating large language models into Java applications. Whether you're already using LangChain4j in production or just starting to explore its capabilities, this session is a great opportunity to connect with fellow developers, contributors, and enthusiasts. We'll discuss the current state of the project, real-world adoption stories, ongoing challenges, and exciting new developments on the roadmap. This is your chance to ask questions, share feedback, exchange ideas, and help shape the future of LangChain4j. Come with curiosity and leave with insights, connections, and inspiration!
cfpSummary: An open BOF session on LangChain4j’s evolution, adoption, challenges, and roadmap. Join community members to discuss real-world use, share feedback, ask questions, and help shape the future of this fast-growing Java framework for integrating large language models.

title: Measuring the Unmeasurable: Evaluating Generative AI in Practice
abstract:
Getting a generative AI prototype to impress a demo audience is easy. Getting it to behave reliably in production is another story. In production, you don't control what users ask or what the model answers. That's not a bug, that's the whole point of using LLMs. But it is also what makes evaluation genuinely hard, and what separates a convincing proof of concept from a trustworthy production system.

This session tackles the core paradox of building with large language models: how do you harness their creativity while maintaining control over their outputs? We will use a RAG-based chatbot as our running example, a real-world case where you have to guarantee output quality without ever controlling what users actually ask, and where linguistic fluency and factual accuracy constantly pull in opposite directions, to show what a complete, reproducible evaluation pipeline actually looks like in practice.

Along the way, we will cover why traditional metrics fall short, how to use LLMs as judges and where that approach quietly fails, when human evaluation is non-negotiable, and how to set up continuous monitoring to catch drift before your users do.

You will leave with practical frameworks and a clear methodology to make evaluation a constant driver of development, from the first prototype to the last production release.
cfpSummary: This session explores how to evaluate generative AI systems reliably despite their unpredictability. Using a RAG chatbot case study, it covers adapting metrics for accuracy, coherence, and business value; the limits of traditional and LLM-as-a-judge methods; the role of human review; and continuous monitoring for drift.

speakers.name: Erin Pacquetet
speakers.bio:
Erin Pacquetet is a Senior AI and Data Scientist at SCIAM, where she designs, develops, and deploys production-grade AI products.
At the intersection of linguistics and computer science, she brings a creative, human-centered approach to hard engineering problems, translating product challenges into robust, scalable AI architectures that work for both technical teams and business stakeholders.
Her expertise spans prompt design and optimization, advanced data pipeline management, model evaluation, and the integration of industrial-grade AI systems.
Beyond her industry work, Erin is an active researcher and community contributor. She regularly speaks at meetups and conferences on topics including AI model analysis, pragmatic AI integration in software development, and human–machine interaction through language.

videoTitle: Measuring the Unmeasurable: Evaluating Generative AI in Practice  by Erin Pacquetet

title: 🚀 From Java to AI: Build Your First Intelligent Agent System!
abstract:
🎯 Revolutionize the way you see Java development with AI!
You know Java? Then you already hold 80% of the keys to building sophisticated AI systems. Don't let Python monopolize innovation: with LangChain4j, Java becomes the go-to language for production-grade AI.

On the agenda for this hands-on workshop:

🧱 Part 1: AI as a Service. Learn to inject intelligence via CDI just like any other Bean. Manage conversational memory with scopes (@SessionScoped) and give your agents "arms" through Function Calling.

🏗️ Part 2: The Agent Architect. Go beyond simple chat. Design complex declarative workflows (sequential, parallel) and master the Supervisor Pattern: an AI capable of planning and managing other agents autonomously.

🚀 Why attend? Walk away with ready-to-use patterns, a solid grasp of the MCP/A2A protocols, and the ability to integrate robust agents into your enterprise architectures.
Go from spectator to AI architect! 🚀
cfpSummary: Hands-on workshop on building production-grade AI in Java with LangChain4j. Learn CDI-based AI injection, conversational memory, function calling, declarative agent workflows, and the Supervisor Pattern. Gain practical patterns, MCP/A2A protocol knowledge, and skills to integrate robust AI agents into enterprise architectures.

He is no stranger to the Devoxx stage: he ran two Hands-on Labs at Devoxx France (2012 and 2015) on Java EE, and more recently delivered a Hands-on Lab on Quarkus and Apache Ignite at Riviera Dev, Devoxx BE, and Devoxx MA in 2023. In 2026, together with Antoine Sabot-Durand, he built Vidocq (https://vidocq.dev) — the first fully European MicroProfile 7.1 runtime.

title: Open Source in the Age of AI: Where's the value?
abstract:
While some folks believe Open Source is important to do Because It's The Right Thing To Do, others have been able to persuade their organisations to open source valuable IP because it brings something to the company. Still others have been able to make money off an open source project they started.

Has this changed in the age of AI? If AI is being trained on open source and freely available code, does that make open source libraries and tools more or less valuable? Can an organisation still make money off their open source tools if AI agents can just go ahead and create code for them without needing training, consulting or support contracts?

Or was the value never in the money it brought, but in the community story? Making your code freely available, creating useful documentation and example code, supporting the community that grows around your open source tool might be the real goal, not simply the path to the destination.

Trisha wants to bring together open source maintainers, contributors and enthusiasts to discuss difficult questions around running an open source tool. Like:
  • How does it support itself financially?
  • How do you decide what belongs in an open source offering vs what should be commercial/paid?
  • Why do we create open source tools in the first place?
  • What are the pros and cons of having open source tools in an AI world?
  • How do we build businesses around open source tools?
  • How do we use open source tools to support businesses?
cfpSummary: This talk explores how AI changes the value of open source, asking whether libraries and tools remain commercially useful when AI can generate code. It brings together maintainers and contributors to discuss funding, community, business models, and the purpose of open source in an AI-driven world.

speakers.name: Trisha Gee
speakers.bio:
Trisha Gee is a Java Champion, author, and internationally recognised speaker who has spent over 20 years building software and helping developers build it better. From high-performance financial systems to developer tools, she brings hands-on experience and a clear, practical perspective on what actually makes teams effective, and how engineering organisations build better software.

She is the co-author of Head First Java and Getting to Know IntelliJ IDEA, and her talks, articles, and videos are widely used by developers to navigate complex topics and improve how they work. She focuses on developer productivity, proven engineering practices, and the role of human judgment in an increasingly AI-assisted world.

Trisha got her start in developer communities, founding and supporting user groups and engaging directly with developers. She continues to champion community-led learning, inclusive practices, and the idea that great software comes from people, not just tools.

title: The Quantum Tech Lead: Hands-On and Abstract at the Same Time
abstract:
So you got "promoted" to lead a team / project / whatever. What now? Do you have what it takes? It certainly seems that your hierarchy thinks so. But oftentimes things are not so black and white. Being a great plumber doesn't automatically make you a great leader of plumbers, so you need to adapt and adjust your ways of working by dropping old habits and picking up new ones. Then you start getting worried by the fact that you won't be able to have as much impact as before, since you're not coding as much as you used to in the past (and that's what you're good at, right?).

What if leadership can amplify your technical impact instead? In this talk, I’ll share how I evolved from individual contributor to a mix of Solution Architect, Tech Lead and classical Engineering Manager at CERN - keeping my hands in the code while scaling my influence through the team that I work with. I'll be sharing best practices and adjustment techniques for you to use when faced with the difficult transition process into technical leadership. And lastly, we'll be talking about how to stay relevant even if you're not spending countless hours honing your coding skills anymore.
cfpSummary: This talk explores the transition from individual contributor to technical leader, showing how leadership can amplify impact rather than reduce it. Drawing on experience at CERN, it shares practical techniques for adapting, staying relevant, and maintaining technical influence while leading teams.

speakers.name: Cristian Schuszter
speakers.bio:
Dr. Cristian Schuszter holds a PhD in Systems Engineering with a focus on distributed fault-tolerant software architectures and machine-learning based failure prediction. In his day-to-day, he is somewhere between a Data and Full-stack Software Engineer, with a wide range of tech & job exposure both in academia and industry.

For the past 8 years he's been working with various teams in CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research). Currently he's focusing on the architectural directions of the CERN business computing group, with an emphasis on enterprise Java systems and UI.

title: Knocking on the Wrong Door: The Six Developers You’ll Meet in Security
abstract:
Secure by Design does not fail only because developers lack security awareness. It often fails because teams prescribe the wrong intervention: training when the real blocker is time, tools, motivation, or trust. In this practitioner-focused talk, we introduce SECUR-E, the OWASP Security Culture Project v2.0 framework that uses COM-B to help developers and software teams diagnose what actually blocks secure development behavior.

Through a relatable story, practical examples, and six memorable developer patterns, Skeptic, Enthusiast, Compliant, Unaware, Resistant, and Embedded, the audience will learn why one-size-fits-all security programs miss, bore, or backfire. We will show how a lightweight self-assessment maps Capability, Opportunity, and Motivation into team insights, then translates those insights into better interventions: evidence for Skeptics, support for Enthusiasts, autonomy for Resistant profiles, foundational help for Unaware developers, and amplification for Embedded security-minded builders.

Key takeaways: stop asking “why don’t developers care?”; diagnose whether the blocker is skill, environment, or motivation; choose interventions that fit the pattern; protect psychological safety; and use SECUR-E as a practical playbook for building secure software teams without blame. Audience: software developers, tech leads, security champions, and engineering managers with beginner-to-intermediate knowledge.
cfpSummary: SECUR-E, an OWASP framework using COM-B, helps teams diagnose why secure development fails—whether due to skills, environment, or motivation—not just awareness. It identifies six developer patterns and guides tailored interventions, improving secure software practices without blame.

speakers.name: Enrique Larios Vargas
speakers.bio: Enrique Larios Vargas is a Security and Learning Specialist with over 8 years of experience designing impactful learning and enablement programs across fintech, engineering, and security domains. With a background as a university lecturer in software engineering in Peru, the Netherlands, and Canada, he brings a unique blend of technical insight and behavioral science to his work. Enrique is the lead author of the research paper “DASP: A Framework for Driving the Adoption of Software Security Practices”, which explores how behavioral models like COM-B can drive secure development. He is passionate about helping developers move beyond compliance and build a meaningful, human-centered security culture.

videoTitle: Knocking on the Wrong Door: The Six Developers You’ll Meet in Security  by Enrique Larios Vargas

title: Beyond encryption at rest: computing on encrypted data
abstract:
Cloud providers encrypt data at rest and in transit, but most applications still decrypt information before processing it. Homomorphic Encryption (HE) challenges this model by allowing computations to be performed directly on encrypted data: the server computes the result without ever seeing the inputs.
This talk introduces the fundamentals of HE, from early partially homomorphic cryptosystems to Craig Gentry's 2009 breakthrough, explaining core concepts like ciphertext noise, noise budgets, and bootstrapping in an accessible way. We'll cover how modern schemes like CKKS, BGV, and TFHE differ in what they compute efficiently, and explore practical use cases: confidential AI inference where a model produces predictions without seeing user inputs and financial services where credit scoring operates entirely on encrypted records.
We'll also discuss current limitations (performance overhead, ciphertext size, and developer complexity) and how hardware acceleration and compiler tooling are rapidly closing these gaps. Attendees will leave with a clear picture of where HE is practical today and where it is not, and concrete pointers to start experimenting with open-source libraries.
cfpSummary: This talk explains Homomorphic Encryption, which enables computation on encrypted data without decryption. It covers core concepts, modern Fully Homomorphic Encryption, practical applications in confidential AI, healthcare, and finance, and current limitations such as performance, ciphertext size, and implementation complexity.

speakers.name: Andrea Iacono
speakers.bio: Andrea is a software engineer with a broad experience in several industries ranging from e-commerce to industrial automation, from public administration to Web TV / music. His interests are in algorithms, data and AI.

videoTitle: Beyond encryption at rest: computing on encrypted data  by Andrea Iacono

title: G1, ZGC, Shenandoah, ... with all these GCs in Java, which one do I choose?
abstract:
It feels like with every new Java release, there are more and more Garbage Collectors (GCs) coming with more and more options. We hear cryptic phrases like: "Oh, awesome, ZGC became generational while Shenandoah isn't" or "Did you heard how Netflix reduced their tail latencies with ZGC?"

Naturally, it leaves us with a ton of questions:
  • What on earth are they talking about?
  • What exactly is ZGC?
  • If this ZGC is so magical, why are there even other GCs left in Java anyway?
  • Why do we only ever talk about different GCs for Java, but never for Go or JavaScript? Can the Java folks make up their minds and pick one?
  • And what about native? Do we even need a GC there?

Whether you are a Java developer or just plain curious, everyone is welcome! We will trace the journey from the creation of Java all the way to the present day to understand why we need a GC and why it isn't a solved problem. We will also take a tour of the various GCs, their evolutions, their strengths, and their weaknesses. (Spoiler alert: ZGC is not the one GC to rule them all).

By the end of this talk, you will know exactly when to use which GC so you can find the perfect fit for every project, every application, and every environment.
cfpSummary: This talk explains why Java has multiple garbage collectors, what ZGC, Shenandoah, and others do, and their strengths and weaknesses. It traces GC history, compares alternatives, and shows when to use each one for the right project, application, or environment.

speakers.name: Antoine DESSAIGNE
speakers.bio:
A Java developer with over 20 years of experience, Antoine has been a key part of Axway since 2012.

He dedicated 13 years to their Analytics software, evolving from developer to software architect while maintaining a hands-on development role. His final five years on the project were focused on performance optimization, cloud migration, and security.

Antoine is passionate about open source and reports bugs to community-driven projects. He is always eager to migrate to the latest JDK and introduce new features to his team.

Today, he is leveraging his expertise to build an AI Gateway solution, tackling complex code, and mentoring others.

videoTitle: G1, ZGC, Shenandoah,     with all these GCs in Java, which one do I choose?  by Antoine DESSAIGNE

title: Specialized AI Agents: from concept to production
abstract:
More and more of us use **Coding Assistants** that excel at **writing code**.

They are **good** and they are **expensive**!

For our business needs, we need **more specialised AI agents** that are as good
or ever better, but for a much **cheaper** price.

The same underlying models can be used to write
more **specialized, cheaper, more predictable AI agents**.

We'll start by writing very disposable agents in literally seconds, **without code**.

And then we'll demonstrate how to grow such agent into solving a real business case.
We'll iterate on the agent, we'll give it tools and then we'll evaluate it and optimize it with **solid evals**.
We'll monitor its costs and see how changing models help or degrade.

Finally, we'll discover how multiple agents can connect and collaborate in production
with **MCP, ACP and A2A**.

All of that can be done with almost no code, leveraging [Docker Agent](https://docker.github.io/docker-agent/),
an open-source project and a real Swiss Army knife for AI agent creation.
cfpSummary: The proposal shows how to build cheaper, specialized AI agents with minimal code using Docker Agent. It covers creating disposable agents quickly, iterating to solve real business problems, adding tools, evaluating and optimizing performance, monitoring costs, and connecting multiple agents for production collaboration.

speakers.name: David Gageot
speakers.bio: Engineer at Docker, working an AI agents.

videoTitle: Specialized AI Agents: from concept to production  by David Gageot

title: Deterministic by Design - Achieving Reproducible Builds with Maven
abstract:
Modern software delivery pipelines face increasing pressure from auditors, regulators, and internal governance teams. Yet many builds remain non‑reproducible. This lack of determinism creates blind spots in compliance, undermines traceability, and exposes organisations to risks when validating what actually went into production.

This session demonstrates how developers can use Apache Maven features to reliably produce identical artifacts from identical inputs. You’ll also learn how to diagnose where reproducibility breaks down and how Maven’s built‑in verification tools can highlight sources of non‑determinism.

Join this talk to understand why reproducibility is becoming a non‑negotiable requirement for responsible software development and what you can do to make your build deterministic by design.
cfpSummary: This session shows how Apache Maven can make builds reproducible by producing identical artifacts from identical inputs. It explains how to diagnose non-determinism, use Maven’s verification tools, and improve traceability and compliance in software delivery pipelines increasingly scrutinized by auditors and regulators.

speakers.name: Maarten Mulders
speakers.bio: Maarten is a solution architect, senior Java developer, and technical trainer with a passion for developer productivity and software quality. He is recognised as a Java Champion and Oracle ACE Pro for his contributions to the Java community through speaking, mentoring, and content creation. Maarten is passionate about "building the right thing" and "building the thing right". He loves to share new ideas and knowledge through speaking and his blog. When he's not writing code or speaking at conferences, Maarten enjoys exploring creativity through photography, music, and experimenting in the kitchen - in no particular order.

videoTitle: Deterministic by Design   Achieving Reproducible Builds with Maven  by Maarten Mulders

title: AI in the Dark: Running LLMs in Air-Gapped Production Environments
abstract:
Building an AI agent is easy. Building one you'd trust in production is harder. Building one that runs with no internet access, no cloud APIs, and no external services: that's a different problem entirely.

This talk follows a real journey: taking an AI-driven service from demo to production in an air-gapped defence environment where OpenAI, Azure and others are simply not an option.

The cloud disappearing changes everything: local LLMs under real performance constraints, tool-calling without external infrastructure, hallucination you can't fix by swapping an API, and human oversight in a system that talks to nothing outside its own network.

This is a production story from an environment where "it works on my machine" was never good enough and that's because the machine is isolated, locked down, and the usual shortcuts don't exist.
cfpSummary: This talk describes moving an AI service from demo to production in an air-gapped defence environment with no internet, cloud APIs, or external services. It covers local LLM constraints, offline tool-calling, hallucination risks, and the need for human oversight in a fully isolated system.

speakers.name: Mihaela Gheorghe-Roman
speakers.bio:

In her professional career, spanning over 15 years, she has worked in the telecom and defence domains with a focus on Java, Spring Boot, C, C#, Scala and Angular, and a growing interest in AI systems and agentic architectures.

Outside of tech, she holds a black belt in traditional Jiu-Jitsu, runs marathons, and travels the world whenever she gets the chance.

videoTitle: AI in the Dark: Running LLMs in Air Gapped Production Environments by Mihaela Gheorghe Roman

title: "You May Now Optimize the Wedding": Optimizing the Seating, Bachelor Party, and Honeymoon with Constraint AI
abstract:
Every developer has been there: sitting at a life event, thinking "could I automate this?" The answer is yes. And this talk will show you how.

There is a whole class of problems that AI alone cannot solve: scheduling, routing, and planning challenges where every decision affects every other decision. Timefold tackles these in production every day, across logistics, manufacturing, healthcare, and yes, apparently also weddings.

We will use the most important weekend of your life as our excuse to explore constraint optimization in practice, from seating charts to pub crawls to honeymoon itineraries, with real code, real constraints, and real solver magic.
You will leave knowing how to turn any "could I automate this?" moment into a working optimization solution.
cfpSummary: This talk shows how to automate complex planning problems using constraint optimization. Using wedding scenarios like seating charts, pub crawls, and honeymoon itineraries, it demonstrates how Timefold solves scheduling, routing, and planning challenges with real code and constraints, turning “could I automate this?” into working optimization solutions.

speakers.bio:

His technology is in use across the globe, to automate complex scheduling and routing of hundreds of thousands of employees, vehicles and machinery every day.

title: Beyond the Pod: Architecting and Scaling AI Agents on Kubernetes
abstract:
As we shift from simple LLM wrappers to autonomous AI agents, a critical question emerges: Where and how should they run? On Kubernetes, our instinct is to treat agents like traditional microservices, giving each its own Pod for isolation and identity. But AI agents aren’t microservices.

Unlike long-running APIs, agents are ephemeral, bursty, and highly stateful. They might spin up for a task, spawn parallel sub-agents, and then sit idle for hours awaiting human approval. Keeping a dedicated Pod alive for every agent is massively wasteful.

In this talk, we’ll explore Agent Substrate, an open-source system on Kubernetes that decouples the logical agent ("Actor") from the physical execution environment ("Worker" Pod).

What you will learn:
  • Heavy Multiplexing: Map thousands of stateful, idle AI agents onto a small pool of shared Kubernetes Pods.
  • Hibernate and Teleport: Look under the hood at how Substrate uses OCI containers and gVisor to achieve sub-second activation, session teleportation, and perfect state persistence across hibernation.
  • Rethink Identity & Security: Shift network policies and access controls away from the Pod level and attach them dynamically to lightweight execution units.

Leave this session with a fresh perspective on how to isolate and scale the next generation of AI applications without abandoning the Kubernetes ecosystem you already know.
cfpSummary: This talk presents Agent Substrate, a Kubernetes system that separates logical AI agents from physical Pods. It enables thousands of stateful, idle agents to share resources efficiently, with hibernation, rapid activation, session teleportation, and dynamic security controls for scalable, isolated AI applications.

title: Faster Development with Java, Python, and Micronaut
abstract:
The Java platform has always been about performance, reliability, and a rich developer ecosystem. But what if those same capabilities could become the foundation for building modern polyglot applications?

In this session, we'll unveil a new pre-compiled, pre-optimized Micronaut runtime built on GraalVM that delivers fast startup, low memory footprint, and a consistent programming model across Java, Kotlin, Python, and other Micronaut-supported languages.

Unlike approaches that require expensive native image builds before you see the benefits, this runtime is pre-compiled ahead of time, keeping the developer feedback loop fast. Make a source change, restart, and you're back in milliseconds—while still taking advantage of GraalVM's performance and native deployment capabilities when you're ready for production.

You'll see how Micronaut's dependency injection, configuration, testing, observability, and cloud-native features extend naturally across languages, enabling polyglot applications without sacrificing operational consistency. We'll also explore why this architecture is an ideal fit for AI-powered systems, combining Java's production strengths with the flexibility of Python where it makes sense.

If you're interested in the future of Java, GraalVM, cloud-native runtimes, and the next generation of polyglot application development, this session offers an early look at what's coming next.
cfpSummary: This talk shows how Micronaut, GraalPy, and GraalVM let Python gain Java’s structure, tooling, and native performance without losing simplicity. It explores building polyglot applications, integrating Python and Java cleanly, and using AI to enhance workflows and developer experiences.

speakers.name: Graeme Rocher
speakers.bio: Graeme Rocher is the creator of several popular Open Source projects including Grails (https://grails.org) and Micronaut (https://Micronaut.io) and co-author of "The Definitive Guide to Grails" (Springer - https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4302-0871-6). Graeme currently works as an Architect at Oracle. Graeme is a member of the Java Champions (https://twitter.com/java_champions) and 2018 was awarded the Groundbreaker award by Oracle (https://developer.oracle.com/groundbreakers/) for his work on Open Source.

speakers.name: Thomas Wuerthinger
speakers.bio: Thomas Wuerthinger is a Vice President at Oracle leading programming language implementation teams for languages including Python, JavaScript, and Java. He is the architect of the Graal compiler and the Truffle self-optimizing runtime system. Previously, he worked on the Crankshaft optimizing compiler of V8 at Google, and the Maxine research virtual machine at Sun Microsystems. He received a PhD degree from JKU Linz for his research about dynamic code evolution.

videoTitle: Faster Development with Java, Python, and Micronaut  by Graeme Rocher, Thomas Wuerthinger

title: Dream Machines & Walled Gardens
abstract:
Ted Nelson was a troublemaker. In 1974, frustrated by the closed and bureaucratic world of computing, he wrote Computer Lib/Dream Machines, a book that was part manifesto and part blueprint for a digital future. Nelson saw computers not as tools of control but as portals to personal freedom, creativity and interconnected knowledge. He championed hypertext long before the web, called out the dangers of technical jargon designed to exclude ordinary people and fought for systems that put users in charge.

This talk tells the story of Computer Lib, the man behind it and the philosophy that shaped it. It explores how Nelson’s ideas could have led to a very different digital world, one built around open, decentralised knowledge rather than the walled gardens and algorithmic control we have today. What if his vision had won? What would the internet look like if computing had followed the path of Computer Lib instead of Big Tech?

Nelson once wrote that “most authority is malignant.” This is a talk about the man who wanted to dismantle it and the future we lost when the world ignored him.
cfpSummary: The talk profiles Ted Nelson and his 1974 manifesto *Computer Lib/Dream Machines*, which envisioned computers as tools for freedom, creativity, and open hypertext. It asks how the internet might differ today if Nelson’s user-centered, decentralized vision had prevailed over Big Tech’s closed, algorithmic systems.

speakers.name: Anders Norås
speakers.bio:
Anders Norås started out in arts and design, but for the last 25 years he has been creating magic with code instead of paint. Blending creativity with technical skill, he brings a perspective on technology that is as much about people as it is about software.

He has given more than 100 talks at conferences around the world. His presentations are not just lectures, they are experiences. With a sharp delivery and high energy, Anders turns even dry technical material into something lively, memorable and often funny.

Whether you are into computer science, design, media or anything else, Anders offers insights that will make you think and probably make you laugh. He does not just talk about technology. He brings it to life.

videoTitle: Dream Machines & Walled Gardens  by Anders Norås

title: The Rise of Agent Enablement: Coding Agents Don't Scale Themselves. Neither Do Your Teams.
abstract:
In 2009, every big enterprise said "continuous delivery won't work here." In 2026, the same rooms say "the dark factory won't work here." It was never about the technology being ready. It's about the organization being ready. Readiness is a socio-technical problem, not a technical one.

This talk applies Conway's Law all the way up, through four layers of enablement:

0. Enable the agent : this is where the tech is standing today (context + harness).
1. Enable the team : the new mentality of fixing system instead of the code, the changing role, winning over skeptics, new planning/retro ceremonies, and measuring evolution by human-touches-down and sharing-up.
2. Enable the platform: the shared context, harness and infra substrate teams and agents both stand on: model routing, MCP gateways, sandboxes, skill/harness registries, evals, guardrails, paved roads that stay easy paths (not cages), and FinOps that optimizes rather than caps.
3. Enable the organization: the VP of Engineering's job: hiring and interviewing for the new roles, defending a maturing ROI, right-sizing teams, keeping humans able to judge in the "dim factory," and building the real moat : capturing knowledge.

**Target audience**:
Engineering leaders, platform/DevEx engineers, and senior ICs driving agentic-coding adoption. It's for anyone past "we gave them coding tools" and asking why it isn't scaling across the org.
cfpSummary: The talk argues that “dark factory” readiness is organizational, not technical. Using Conway’s Law, it outlines four enablement layers: agent, team, platform, and organization. It targets engineering leaders scaling agentic coding beyond tools, focusing on roles, rituals, infrastructure, ROI, and knowledge capture.

title: Engineering Lessons from Working on Software Older Than Me
abstract:
What do you learn after spending years maintaining and evolving a technology that predates modern programming languages, cloud platforms, and smartphones?

This session explores real engineering challenges encountered while building PDF technology at scale, from compatibility and performance to security, testing, and interoperability. Through a series of stories and hard-earned lessons, you'll see why mature systems can be some of the best teachers for designing resilient software and why the hardest problems are often the ones users never notice.
cfpSummary: A session on engineering lessons from maintaining and scaling legacy PDF technology, covering compatibility, performance, security, testing, and interoperability. It shows how mature systems teach resilient software design and highlights the invisible challenges behind reliable user experiences.

speakers.name: Guust Ysebie
speakers.bio: Software engineer at Apryse, specializing in PDF technologies and the iText SDK. With nearly 7 years of experience in backend development, he works on core PDF internals, standards compliance.

title: Keeping Spring Applications Secure in the Age of AI
abstract:
Spring is the most widely used Java framework in the world, and millions of applications depend on it. Keeping
them up to date used to be a matter of discipline. That has changed. In August 2026 alone, 96 security
vulnerabilities were published in the Spring ecosystem, driven by AI-assisted research. Models such as
Anthropic's Mythos find weaknesses that survived years of manual review, and attackers can use the same
capability.
In this session, we look at what this means for teams running Spring in production and how to respond. We
show how Long Term Support releases for Spring ease the pressure of constant upgrades, how Spring
Application Advisor automates patching and upgrades inside your CI pipeline, and how direct access to the
Spring team helps when automation is not enough. All of this is part of VMware Tanzu Spring, delivered by the
vendor of Spring itself. Customers like SAP rely on exactly this combination to keep their most complex
applications secure and current.
cfpSummary: AI-assisted research is rapidly uncovering Spring vulnerabilities, increasing upgrade pressure. This session explains how Spring teams can respond using Long Term Support releases, Spring Application Advisor for automated CI patching and upgrades, and direct support from the Spring team through VMware Tanzu Spring.

speakers.name: Neven Cvetkovic
speakers.bio: Neven Cvetkovic is a seasoned veteran of the Java ecosystem with over 20 years of experience tackling complex enterprise Dev, Sec, and Ops challenges. At VMware Tanzu, he guides Fortune 2000 organizations through their cloud-native journeys and helps them build, deploy, and scale enterprise AI workloads. Neven is passionate about AI engineering and regularly shares his hard-earned knowledge to help development teams modernize application architectures effectively.

videoTitle: Keeping Spring Applications Secure in the Age of AI  by Neven Cvetkovic
